summary: Automated valuation is the sector's oldest deployed AI, and it is now formally regulated: federal quality-control standards for AVMs took effect in 2025. Valuation, leasing automation, 3D capture, and property operations are where AI actually runs; the regulator record and the platforms' own model documentation are the sources.

analysis.body:
Per the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, 28.9% of firms in real estate and rental and leasing reported using AI in the most recent period, up from 28.0% in the prior period, making this one of the more measurable adoption readings available for the sector. The figure covers the broad NAICS 53 category and reflects firms answering yes to using AI in the previous two weeks, so it captures active deployment rather than intention.

The oldest and most widespread AI application in the sector is automated valuation. Zillow publishes Zestimate valuations for more than 110 million homes using a neural network model that draws on county and tax assessor records, MLS feeds, and listing signals, with Zestimates for most homes updating multiple times per week. HouseCanary offers AI-powered valuations and forecasts covering over 136 million U.S. properties, combining machine learning algorithms with image recognition that identifies room types and assesses home condition from photos. Opendoor uses pricing models to make direct purchase offers to homeowners, a use case where valuation errors carry direct balance-sheet consequences rather than merely advisory ones.

Automated valuation models are now the subject of binding federal regulation. The CFPB, FHFA, OCC, Federal Reserve Board, FDIC, and NCUA jointly finalized a rule implementing quality control standards for AVMs used by mortgage originators and secondary market issuers to determine collateral worth on mortgages secured by a consumer's principal dwelling. Under that rule, institutions must adopt policies and control systems ensuring AVMs maintain a high level of confidence in their estimates, protect against data manipulation, avoid conflicts of interest, and require random sample testing and reviews. This represents the first binding federal framework specifically governing the sector's core AI, and any firm using AVMs in covered credit or securitization decisions must comply.

Beyond valuation, AI is being applied across leasing communications, property operations, and document processing. EliseAI operates as an agentic conversational AI platform that handles messages, calls, tour scheduling, prospect follow-up, and maintenance requests around the clock for property management and housing operators, with the stated aim of cutting overhead and freeing staff for higher-value work. Prophia applies document AI to commercial lease abstraction, extracting key terms and rent roll data from leases and combining that output with expert validation to produce structured portfolio data. Building Engines, a JLL company, embeds AI in its Prism property management platform to deliver instant answers, recommendations, and automation for commercial property teams, with net operating income growth cited as the operational objective. Matterport's 3D capture and computer vision tools digitize physical space into virtual tours, floor plans, and portfolio management data, with integrations into Procore and Autodesk for construction workflows.

On the enterprise and capital side, JLL states it has invested more in AI technology than any other real estate company, deploying it across brokerage, facilities management, and portfolio analytics. The National Association of Realtors maintains technology research tracking agent and brokerage adoption, and its REACH program, operated through Second Century Ventures, functions as an accelerator vetting residential proptech tools. CRETI maintains a network of over 500 investors focused on real estate technology and runs a zero-equity accelerator for emerging companies, making it a useful barometer for where proptech funding concentrates. CREtech convenes commercial real estate leaders specifically around AI deployment, with its New York conference drawing owners, developers, investors, and operators who are actively deploying AI across portfolios.

For a decision-maker weighing deployment, the sector's evidence base is clearer in some areas than others. Valuation AI has the longest production history and the most public methodology documentation, but it now carries explicit federal compliance obligations that require internal governance infrastructure, not just model access. Leasing and operations automation has a growing vendor market with ROI framed around cost reduction and staff efficiency, though independently verified outcome data is limited in what the sources disclose. The regulatory posture is tightening specifically around consumer-facing valuation, and firms using AVMs in mortgage contexts should treat compliance with the interagency quality control rule as a prerequisite rather than an afterthought.
